ABSTRACT Aims Diagnosis of inclusion body myositis (IBM) is difficult and currently based on a combination of clinical and (immuno)histological findings. Biomarkers facilitating the diagnostic process are needed. Alpha‐synuclein (αSN) aggregates are a known histological feature of IBM, but there is a lack of information on their diagnostic relevance. Furthermore, serum αSN concentrations in IBM have not been investigated. Methods Immunohistochemical staining for αSN was performed on 63 biopsies (19 IBM, 21 other inflammatory myopathies, 20 other myopathies and 3 healthy controls), and αSN reactive fibres were quantified. The serum concentration of αSN was determined by ELISA in 156 serum samples (11 IBM, 25 other inflammatory myopathies, 53 hereditary myopathies, 30 mitochondriopathies and 37 healthy controls). Results The proportion of fibres with αSN immunoreactivity was significantly higher in IBM compared to all groups ( p < 0.001) and discriminated IBM against all other neuromuscular disorders with a sensitivity of 79% and a specificity of 85%, which further improved when only non‐regenerating fibres were examined. In serum, αSN concentrations in IBM were generally not different from healthy controls. However, serum concentrations were inversely correlated with disease duration ( r = −0.62, p = 0.04) and positively correlated with the IBM functional rating scale ( r = 0.74, p = 0.01). Consequently, stratification according to these clinical parameters showed significantly lower serum αSN concentrations in late‐stage, more severely affected patients. Conclusions αSN reactivity may serve as an additional immunohistochemical marker for IBM diagnosis. Furthermore, this study indicates that αSN serum concentrations decrease with disease duration and clinical deterioration. Therefore, serum αSN may be provisionally considered a monitoring biomarker in IBM, pending further studies. We examined alpha‐synuclein in muscle and serum samples of patients with IBM and other neuromuscular disorders. With the use of immunohistochemistry, we identify alpha‐synuclein muscular reactivity as a complementary diagnostic marker. Tobias Mayer and Leila Scholle contributed equally to this study. Summary Muscle fibres with alpha‐synuclein‐immunoreactive inclusions are more frequent in inclusion body myositis (IBM) than in non–IBM inflammatory myopathies, other myopathies and healthy controls. Alpha‐synuclein immunohistochemical staining of muscle biopsies has sufficient sensitivity (79%) and specificity (81%) to differentiate IBM from other inflammatory myopathies. Regenerating muscle fibres account for a proportion of alpha‐synuclein‐reactive muscle fibres, the exclusion of which results in higher sensitivity (84%) and specificity (86%) for distinguishing IBM from other inflammatory myopathies. Serum alpha‐synuclein concentrations are generally not altered in IBM but correlate with disease duration and clinical severity. Serum alpha‐synuclein may qualify as a monitoring biomarker in IBM.

extracted_data.document_summary: This comprehensive study investigated alpha-synuclein (αSN) as a potential diagnostic and monitoring biomarker for Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM). It evaluated αSN immunoreactivity in muscle biopsies and its concentration in serum and muscle homogenates, comparing IBM patients to other myopathies and healthy controls. The findings suggest αSN immunoreactivity in muscle is a promising diagnostic marker, while serum αSN levels could serve as a monitoring biomarker, correlating with disease duration and clinical severity in IBM. The study also explored the diagnostic utility of other established and emerging biomarkers in IBM.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved a multimodal assessment of alpha-synuclein (αSN) levels and immunoreactivity in muscle biopsies, muscle tissue homogenates, and serum samples from various cohorts. Muscle biopsies (N=63, including 19 IBM, 21 other inflammatory myopathies, 20 other myopathies, 3 healthy controls) were analyzed by immunohistochemical staining. Serum samples (N=156, including 11 IBM, 25 other inflammatory myopathies, 53 hereditary myopathies, 30 mitochondriopathies, 37 healthy controls) were assessed by ELISA. Muscle homogenates were also examined (N=17 IBM, N=19 other inflammatory myopathies, N=5 hereditary myopathies, N=2 healthy controls). IBM patients were stratified by disease severity (IBMFRS) and disease duration for serum αSN analysis. No interventional dose or therapeutic comparisons were reported, as the study focused on diagnostic and monitoring biomarker evaluation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher proportion of fibres with αSN immunoreactivity in IBM (14.35% ± 10.32%) compared to all other groups (CTR: 0.09% ± 0.16%, p = 0.0020; IIM: 3.90% ± 4.13%, p = 0.0053; non-rimmed vacuolar myopathies: 0.78% ± 0.97%, p < 0.0001). Discriminates IBM with 79% sensitivity and 85% specificity, improving to 84% sensitivity and 86% specificity when only non-regenerating fibres were examined (cutoff > 4.96% for non-regenerating fibres, AUC = 0.93).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Aggregates are a known histological feature of IBM, indicating a pathological process related to proteostasis disturbance, potentially resembling synucleinopathies. Alpha-synuclein is a presynaptic protein, primarily recognized as the main constituent of Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnostic assessment for Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM) from other neuromuscular disorders (e.g., IIM, myopathies with rimmed vacuoles), particularly in muscle tissue.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May serve as an additional immunohistochemical marker for IBM diagnosis, with diagnostic accuracy potentially similar to established markers like p62 and TDP-43. It indicates the presence and severity of muscle pathology in IBM and correlates significantly with total atrophic fibres (r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and total regenerating fibres (r = 0.72, p < 0.001).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Generally not significantly different from healthy controls (IBM: 44.03 ± 32.47 ng/mL vs CTR: 50.47 ± 34.12 ng/mL, p = 0.53). However, significantly lower concentrations were observed in late-stage IBM (19.86 ± 7.45 ng/mL for > 8 years disease duration) compared to CTR (p = 0.018) and early-stage IBM (64.16 ± 31.52 ng/mL, p = 0.03). Also significantly lower in advanced IBM (18.05 ± 8.97 ng/mL for IBMFRS ≤ 20) compared to CTR (p = 0.041) and IIM (p = 0.019). Inversely correlated with disease duration (r = -0.62, p = 0.046) and positively correlated with the IBM functional rating scale (r = 0.74, p = 0.019) in IBM patients.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Implied role in disease progression and clinical severity in IBM. The mechanism of peripheral blood depletion is speculative, but associated with protein aggregation and potential trapping in aggregates within cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Monitoring disease progression and clinical deterioration in Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM) patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May be provisionally considered a monitoring biomarker in IBM, as concentrations decrease with disease duration and clinical deterioration, correlating with clinical markers of disease severity (IBMFRS).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference in the calculated log-αSN/Hb ratio was observed between IBM (1.33 ± 0.54), CTR (1.21 ± 0.22), IIM (1.36 ± 0.31), and HER (1.41 ± 0.45) (p = 0.79). Multivariate logistic regression revealed no significant associations between αSN and diagnosis (IBM vs. CTR) after accounting for Hb (AUC: 0.74 [95% CI: 0.34–1.00], p = 0.29).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Role in synaptic function; aggregation linked to neurodegenerative diseases; investigated as a marker in myopathies. Its measurement can be confounded by haemolysis, necessitating adjustment.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Differentiation of IBM from other NMDs at the muscle tissue level, after correction for haemolysis.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a differentiating marker for IBM versus other groups in muscle tissue homogenates when corrected for haemolysis. Does not significantly correlate with clinical or histological parameters in this context.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Initial studies reported high specificity (85%–100%), but recent publications have not been able to replicate these findings. Sensitivity varies widely from 36% to 70%.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Autoantibody against cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A, associated with autoimmune processes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Autoimmune features of Inclusion body myositis (IBM) diagnosis.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Diagnostic biomarker for IBM, but with variable and often insufficient specificity and sensitivity, indicating a need for additional markers.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Accumulation identified; considered the most accurate degenerative marker among histological features. More common in biopsies that also show other histological features of advanced disease (e.g., rimmed vacuoles). Previous studies report highly variable sensitivity (12.5%–91%) and specificity (18%–100%) for IBM diagnosis.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: DNA/RNA binding protein, involved in protein processing and degradation, and a marker for protein accumulation indicating a general disturbance of proteostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Muscle degeneration and diagnostic utility in Inclusion body myositis (IBM), particularly in advanced stages and for differentiation from PM-Mito.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Accurate degenerative marker for IBM, but its value may be limited in early disease stages. Established immunopathological marker for IBM, but with variable diagnostic accuracy.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Accumulation identified; considered the most accurate degenerative marker among histological features. More common in biopsies that also show other histological features of advanced disease (e.g., rimmed vacuoles). Previous studies report highly variable sensitivity (12.5%–91%) and specificity (18%–100%) for IBM diagnosis. The pathology observed in IBM is specifically noted as not present in PM-Mito.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Autophagy receptor, involved in protein degradation pathways, and a marker for protein accumulation indicating a general disturbance of proteostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Muscle degeneration and diagnostic utility in Inclusion body myositis (IBM), particularly in advanced stages and for differentiation from PM-Mito.

Established immunopathological marker for IBM, but with variable diagnostic accuracy. Its absence in PM-Mito suggests αSN may have additional value in early stages of IBM.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identified as useful histological features; no quantitative data provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects mitochondrial enzyme activity (Cytochrome c oxidase (COX) and Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)), indicating mitochondrial abnormalities.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnostic histological features in Inclusion body myositis (IBM).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: IIM patients had higher CK activity than all other groups (specific values not provided in this excerpt). Correlated significantly with IBMFRS (r = 0.803, p = 0.012) in IBM patients. Showed a trend towards significant correlation with αSN concentrations (r = 0.62, p = 0.06) in IBM patients.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in energy metabolism, primarily found in muscle; elevated levels often indicate muscle damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis/characterization of Inflammatory Myopathies (IIM) and correlation with IBM severity.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher activity in IIM patients compared to other groups. In IBM, it correlates with IBMFRS, suggesting its utility as an indicator of muscle damage severity or disease burden.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly elevated Hb concentrations observed in all examined tissue homogenate samples; Hb concentration was higher in muscle tissue homogenates compared to serum samples. A slight correlation with αSN was suggested in diseased cohort (r=0.525), but no correlation was observed in healthy controls.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of haemolysis, which can confound α-synuclein measurements in tissue homogenates.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Measurement in muscle homogenates and serum samples during analysis of α-synuclein in Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM) patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels in muscle homogenates indicate haemolysis, necessitating adjustment (e.g., log-αSN/Hb ratio) to accurately reflect actual αSN concentration in muscle cells.
